summary: Describes the Layer Refresh Request (LRR) RTCP Payload-Specific Feedback Message, used to ask for a state refresh of one or more substreams of a layered media stream. It also defines its use with several RTP payload formats.

eli5.summary: Video can be sent in layers. If a layer is damaged, the receiver sends a request to refresh that layer.

questions: what is a layer refresh request
subtitle: A way for a video receiver to ask for a fresh start on just the layers it needs, not the whole stream.

tldr.problem: A receiver that wants to start decoding more layers of a layered video stream has no cheap way to ask. A Full Intra Request would force the whole stream to refresh.
tldr.mechanism: The Layer Refresh Request (LRR) is an RTCP payload-specific feedback message that names a target layer, and optionally the layer the receiver already decodes, so only the layers that need it get a refresh point.
tldr.outcome: Senders must produce a refresh point as soon as possible, within congestion control limits. LRR is meant for deliberate layer upgrades, not for recovering from packet loss.

today: RFC 9627 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is used by the VP9 payload format in RFC 9628.

sections.title: Why Ask for a Layer Refresh
sections.content:
Some video streams are sent in layers. A receiver may decode only some of them and later decide to decode more. To do that it needs a point in the stream from which the extra layers can be decoded without older data it never received.

RFC 9627 defines the Layer Refresh Request (LRR), an RTCP payload-specific feedback message, so a receiver can ask for exactly that. The alternative, a Full Intra Request (FIR), would refresh the entire stream. The RFC says LRR applies to temporally and spatially scaled streams, in single-stream and multi-stream scalability modes.
sections.eli5: If you only want to add one more layer to what you are watching, you should not have to ask for the whole video to restart. LRR lets you ask for just the part you need.

sections.title: Layer Refresh Points
sections.content:
A layer refresh point is a point in a scalable stream after which a decoder that could decode only some of the layers (possibly none) can decode more of them.

For spatial or quality layers, a refresh typically means the layer's picture is encoded to reference only lower-layer pictures of the current picture, not earlier pictures of the same layer. The encoder also promises not to use earlier pictures of that layer as reference in the future. Other layers can keep their dependencies on earlier content, which is the difference from a FIR and keeps the coding overhead small.

For temporal layers, the layer must be temporally nested: it references only earlier frames of a lower temporal layer. In many streams every frame is already nested, and then decoders have no need to send LRR messages.

A layer index is a numeric label made of a temporal-layer ID and a layer ID. How layers are labeled is specific to each codec.
sections.eli5: A refresh point is a spot where a new viewer can jump in on a layer without needing anything older. The rest of the layers can carry on as before.

sections.title: The LRR Message Format
sections.content:
The LRR is identified by RTCP packet type PSFB and FMT value 10. Its Feedback Control Information (FCI) holds one or more entries, one per media sender, each identified by its SSRC. The message length MUST be 2+3*N 32-bit words, where N is the number of entries.

Each entry carries the SSRC, an 8-bit command sequence number, a C flag, a 7-bit payload type, and the layer fields. The sequence number goes up by 1 for each new command (modulo 256) and a repetition does not increase it. The target layer is given by TTID (3 bits) and TLID (8 bits). If C is 1, the current layer is given by CTID and CLID, and the request covers only layers above that. If C is 0, the request covers all layers up to and including the target.

When C is 1 the target MUST be a real upgrade: neither target field may be below its current counterpart, and at least one must be greater. A receiver that gets a request violating this MUST discard it. Reserved bits are set to zero and ignored on reception.
sections.eli5: The request says who it is for, which layer you want, and optionally which layer you already have. It must ask for something higher than what you have, or it gets ignored.

sections.title: How a Sender Responds
sections.content:
In the common RTCP feedback header, the "SSRC of packet sender" is the source of the request, and the "SSRC of media source" is not used and is set to zero. One LRR message may ask several media senders at once, using one entry each.

On receiving an LRR, the encoder MUST send a decoder refresh point as soon as possible. It MUST still respect congestion control limits, which can slow it down because refresh points are often larger than other frames. LRR follows the FIR model for retransmission, reliability and use in multipoint conferences.

An LRR MUST NOT be sent in reaction to picture loss from packet loss or corruption. The RFC recommends a Picture Loss Indication (PLI) instead. LRR SHOULD be used only when the decoder's behavior explicitly changes, for example when it starts decoding a layer it had been discarding.
sections.eli5: The video sender should send a fresh starting point quickly, but not so fast that it clogs the network. And you should not use this to fix glitches, only when you choose to watch more layers.

sections.title: Layer Indices in Specific Codecs
sections.content:
An LRR only works with a scalable codec once that codec's RTP payload format says how the layer fields are laid out and how a receiver recognizes a refresh. New payload specifications for scalable codecs SHOULD define this. The VP9 payload in RFC 9628 already does.

  • H.264 SVC: the layer index holds a temporal ID, a dependency ID and a quality ID. A spatial refresh is seen through the I bit (idr_flag) in the extended NAL unit header, and temporal refresh through Temporal Level Switching Point SEI messages. If the stream's temporal_id_nesting flag is set, receivers SHOULD NOT send temporal LRRs.
  • VP8: only temporal scalability exists. A refresh point is a packet with the Y bit set. Because the Y bit implies a switch of all layers, LRR with VP8 can be somewhat inefficient.
  • H.265: the layer index holds a TID and a layer ID. Temporal refresh is identified by NAL unit types 2 to 5, or by any IRAP picture (types 16 to 23). If the VPS or SPS nesting flag is set, receivers SHOULD NOT send temporal LRRs.
sections.eli5: Each video format labels its layers in its own way, so every format needs to say where the layer numbers go and how to spot the fresh starting point.

sections.title: Transport Modes and SDP Signalling
sections.content:
LRR works with all three scalability transmission mechanisms from RFC 7656: a single RTP stream on a single transport, multiple streams on a single transport, and multiple streams on multiple transports. For the multi-stream cases, the media source SSRC is that of the stream holding the current layer (if C is 1) or the base stream (if C is 0). On receipt, the sender MUST refresh all the requested layers simultaneously in decode order.

Support is signalled in SDP by a new codec control command, lrr, added to the grammar of RFC 5104 as rtcp-fb-ccm-param =/ SP "lrr". The offer/answer rules from RFC 5104 apply. IANA registered lrr in the Codec Control Messages registry and FMT value 10 for LRR in the PSFB registry.
sections.eli5: Endpoints say in their call setup that they understand LRR, using the word lrr, so nobody sends a request the other side cannot read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: All security considerations of FIR feedback packets in RFC 5104 apply to LRR too. In addition, a media sender MUST check that the payload types and layer indices in an LRR are valid for the stream it is sending, and discard the request if not.
sections.eli5: The sender double-checks that a request makes sense for the video it is really sending, and ignores it if it does not.

fields.name: SSRC
fields.desc: SSRC of the media sender asked to send a refresh point.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Whether the current-layer fields are present.

fields.name: Payload Type
fields.desc: Gives the context for interpreting the layer index.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero, ignored on reception.

fields.name: TLID
fields.desc: Target spatial or quality layer ID.

fields.name: CTID
fields.desc: Current temporal-layer ID, if C is 1.

fields.name: CLID
fields.desc: Current layer ID, if C is 1.
